newsitem.title: USA: Dollar slumps on sterling losses, Japan trade data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar slumps on sterling losses, Japan trade data.

text.p: The dollar, battered by heavy selling of U.S. stocks and bonds and a sharp downturn in the British pound against European currencies and the yen, posted its biggest one-day losses in three months on Friday.
The dollar initially weakened in overnight trading after Japan reported its trade surplus widened further in June and a German central banker said the dollar was too strong.

The losses were exacerbated by a second day of heavy selling of the British pound against the Japanese yen and the German mark. Sterling has fallen nearly 5 percent against the mark since Thursday, when the Bank of England said its fourth consecutive monthly increase in official interest rates could be the last for some time.
Higher interest rates tend to boost a currency by lifting the value of investments denominated in that currency.

"Sterling was under severe pressure in early trade and a lot of what's happened to the dollar is related to what's happened in sterling," said Michael Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
However, against the U.S. currency, the pound settled at $1.5875 Friday, unchanged from the previous day.

The dollar fell to 1.8452 marks from 1.8690 marks late on Thursday, its biggest one-day drop since May 20. The dollar settled at 114.80 yen, down from 118.43 yen late on Thursday, its biggest one-day loss since May 9.
The dollar fell to 1.5097 Swiss francs from 1.5305 Swiss francs on Thursday and rose to Canadian $1.3902 from Canadian $1.3882.

Wall Street stocks and bonds also tumbled, compounding the dollar's woes in New York trading. The Dow Jones industrial average fell 156.78 points, or 1.9 percent, to 8,031.22, while the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond slumped to its lowest point since July 2.
"This was a correction, and a big one. Everybody was long in the dollar and U.S. assets," said Andrew Hodge, financial strategist at Bank Brussels Lambert in New York.

The dollar weakened in overnight trading after Japan reported its current account surplus -- the broadest measure of trade in goods and services -- rose 56 percent in June from a year earlier to over one trillion yen.

U.S. officials have repeatedly warned Japan to take steps to reduce exports or increase imports to shrink the trade surplus. The report raised concerns of increasing tensions between the two economic powers.
"The dollar's fall against the yen was related to the current account figures. There are a lot of current concerns about trade," said Malpede.
Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke also hurt the dollar early Friday by repeating that the central bank would prefer to see the dollar significantly lower, near 1.70 marks.

Later in the day, Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing was quoted by Germany's Boersen-Zeitung newspaper as saying German price developments were moving in the wrong direction, suggesting the central bank might raise interest rates to bolster the mark.
"The Germans were sounding fairly aggressive about the dollar and inflation. We were already spiralling down and that added another kick," said Bank Brussels Lambert's Hodge.
A weakening currency raises the price of imported goods, fuelling inflation.
